# Scarrowdale

*A novella*

NovaForge, 2026 — from the premise: *A cartographer is hired to survey a valley that appears on no two maps the same way.*

---

## Synopsis

In 1843, Edmund Hale rides into Scarrowdale to do arithmetic: number every field, seal the plan, collect the fee already owed against his instruments. Four existing surveys of the dale agree on nothing except three fixed points, and no one born here will give him a distance or a bearing — only how long the walk takes, and who last walked it. His chainman hands him the count arrow by arrow rather than speak it aloud. Hale takes the silence for stubbornness, measures the ford stone against the church tower, and rides out satisfied that the dale's reputation is slander. He is wrong before he reaches Ingleford. He returns to find a line he chained twice himself now giving him a different figure on every run, a field corner missing that no one recalls ever being there, and, worst of all, an entry in his own field book, properly witnessed, carrying the parish boundary somewhere he does not remember standing to put it. Silas Brock, the estate's agent, is endlessly obliging about witnessing whatever Hale writes. Hannah Rigg, holding the last good grass under Raven Hause, is the first to tell him plainly what his signature is worth to her. Nothing in Scarrowdale threatens him. Tea is poured. Doors open. The horror is in the columns, and in what a courteous valley can make a careful man believe he wrote himself. A novella about surveys, silence, and the ground a name can take.

**For readers of** *The Loney* by Andrew Michael Hurley, *Piranesi* by Susanna Clarke and Sarah Perry's *The Essex Serpent*.

---

# Chapter 1 — The Ford Stone

The cart came down out of the cloud at the pace of a walking horse, and Edmund Hale saw the dale open beneath him the way a ledger opens: narrow, ruled, and full of entries he had not yet read.

At the mouth of it the beck ran shallow over gravel, and in the gravel stood a stone. It was perhaps four feet out of the water, grey, its top worn to a saddle by a century of cartwheels finding it and shying off. The carter stopped without being asked.

"Sile Ford," he said, which was a name and not a distance, and Hale noted that he said it without complaint.

Hale got down into the water. It came over his boots and he did not mind. He had the chain off the cart before the carter had finished settling the horse, and he walked the first length himself, the brass handles cold, the arrows in his left hand, counting under his breath because there was no one here to count for him. From the stone to the bend of the lane above the ford: two chains, sixty-eight links. He wrote it on his cuff and then, disliking himself for it, copied it nowhere until he had a table.

The satchel held four plans and he spread them on the tailboard with a stone on each corner. The estate plan, drawn for Hollins Hall in a fine tilted hand. The enclosure plan of 1836, which had never been confirmed and did not say why. The turnpike survey, which cared only about the road and had measured everything near it twice. The county plan, which cared about nothing and had measured accordingly.

The ford stone stood on all four. From the stone to the church tower at Nether Scarrow, the estate plan gave a distance; so did the enclosure; so did the turnpike; the county map, being coarser, gave it scaled. Hale laid his dividers across each in turn, and each in turn gave him the same figure within the thickness of the line.

He did that three times. Then he sat on the tailboard with his boots dripping and looked at the four plans, because from the ford stone onward they disagreed about everything else. The Sile did not run the same course on any two of them. A wall that the estate plan ran east of a barn ran west of it on the turnpike. Field corners wandered. Only the stone stayed where it had been put.

"A good mark," he said aloud, and was pleased, because a survey wants a datum and here was one that four men had already agreed upon without meaning to.

---

The lane up was steep and streaming, bracken wet to the knee, cloud sitting on both shoulders of the fell like something laid there. Half a mile up — he thought half a mile; he would chain it — he overtook a woman with a yoke and two milk cans, walking without apparent effort.

"Good day. How far is it to Nether Scarrow?"

"You'll be there before the milk's warm," she said pleasantly.

"I meant in miles."

"It's the same walk my mother did with these cans, and she wasn't quick."

He tried it a third way. "Would you call it more than a mile, or less?"

"I'd call it a walk," she said. "Tom Braithwaite walked it last that wasn't from here, and he wasn't put out by it."

"Is the church straight on, or does the lane turn?"

"The lane goes where it's always gone." She shifted the yoke to her other shoulder and smiled at him with real warmth, as though he had been kind to her. "You'll see the tower when you're meant to."

He stopped asking. It was not rudeness; that was the thing he turned over for the next quarter hour. She had answered every time. She had simply never once given him a number or a bearing, and she had done it the way a person breathes.

---

Nether Scarrow was eleven houses, an inn, and a church whose tower was older than anything else in sight of it. Amos Dent met him in the porch with his coat already on, as if he had been expecting somebody for some days and had not known which day.

The chest under the north window took two keys and a shoulder. Dent lifted out a book bound in calf gone the colour of wet slate, and put it into Hale's hands with both of his, the way a man passes something heavy rather than something precious.

"The perambulation book," he said. "It's yours to keep while you're here. I'd rather it were in the parish than in the Hall."

Hale opened it. The hand was various and old. He read: *thence by the Creed's length to the thorn where Robert Hebblethwaite stood* — and then a gap, and another hand, and *from the thorn to the water as long as a man says the Lord's Prayer twice, John Rigg last walking it*.

"There are no distances in it."

"There's the walk in it," Dent said.

"Will you read me the head of the parish out of it? I'd have it in your voice for the book."

Dent looked at the page for a while. "It's the length of the Creed at a walk, up from the thorn," he said, "and my father walked it last."

"That isn't a direction, Mr Dent."

"No," the vicar agreed, without any embarrassment at all, and locked the empty chest.

---

In the inn parlour that evening Hale laid the four plans side by side on the long table and set a candle at each end, and looked at four different rivers.

The Sile on the estate plan came down the eastern side of the flat ground below the Hause. On the enclosure plan it came down the western. The turnpike had it crossing itself, which it could not do. The county plan had it as a blue thought.

He took out the field book and mixed nothing, the iron-gall being already made up, and wrote in a hand he was proud of:

*11 May 1843. Sile Ford. Ford stone to bend of lane, 2 ch. 68 lks., taken by me. Ford stone agrees with all four plans in relation to the church tower. Nothing else does.*

Then, because a man should know his own position as well as his parish's, he reckoned on the endpaper. Midsummer. The note on the theodolite and the chain fell due at Midsummer, and it was the eleventh of May, and that gave him forty-four days to have a plan sealed, or he would be a bankrupt owning a very good instrument.

The lantern came down the dale at nine, swinging, and Silas Brock came in on the cold with it.

"Mr Hale. Brock, for Hollins Hall." He had the landlord's attention before he had finished his own name, and ordered supper for two. "You'll have found nobody to witness you yet."

"I've been here five hours."

"That's about how long it takes." Brock sat, warm and entirely easy. "I'm not dale-born, sir. Lancaster, same as yourself, they tell me. Which means I can sign what I've stood over, and I'll stand over anything you like at any hour you care to name. Dawn suits me. So does dark."

"I'll want two hands on every entry."

"You'll want a second, and I'm stood here already." Brock cut his meat. "The estate has always understood the head of the parish to be at Raven Hause. I only say it so you know where we think it is. You'll find it where you find it."

He went at eleven. Hale watched the lantern climb until it was a low star going up the fell, then turned back the field book, and wrote in the margin, small:

*check ford stone again on leaving.*

# Chapter 2 — Ten Arrows

The morning came up grey and windless, and by seven the low pastures above Nether Scarrow were steaming where the sun found them. Hale had his station pegged before the dew was off: a stake driven at the corner of the walled ground where the lane met the intake, and beside it the tripod, and on the wall-top his field book in its oilskin.

Nat Fowler came down the lane with the ten arrows in a bundle under his arm and the Ingleford lad trailing behind him, a thin boy of perhaps sixteen named Coulter who had been hired at a shilling the day and had not yet stopped looking at the fell as though it might come nearer. Fowler said good morning. He said the weather would hold till noon and not past it. Then he took the leading end of the chain and went out along the line Hale had set him, and he did not say another word that was not needed.

The chain was Hale's own, a Gunter's of a hundred links, bought new in Lancaster the previous autumn on the same note as the theodolite, and he had tested it twice against a standard and found it honest to a quarter of a link. He liked the sound it made going out — the small iron conversation of the links, then the check, then the silence while Fowler set his arrow and Hale, at the rear, brought the handle up to the mark and read the ground.

They ran the line along the Sile, keeping the beck on their left, the water low and brown over its stones. Fowler was a good chainman. He did not drag and he did not snatch; he laid the chain where Hale's staff told him and he set each arrow upright and clean, pressing it down with the ball of his thumb, and then he walked on. Behind him Coulter drew each arrow as he came to it and passed it forward at the changes. It was the only honest thing Hale had met since he came over the ford, and he let himself enjoy it for the better part of an hour.

At the tenth arrow Fowler stopped and stood waiting.

"Count," Hale said.

Fowler came back along the line, gathering as he came, and Hale watched him do it and understood a moment before it happened that he was not going to hear a number. The chainman stopped an arm's length off. He took Hale's right hand by the wrist, without hurry and without discourtesy, turned it palm up, and laid the arrows into it one after another, iron on skin, until the bundle was all there and cold and his own hands were empty.

"That's what's in your hand, sir," Fowler said. "I'll not say it for you."

Hale stood with the arrows in his palm. Ten of them: he could feel it before he counted, the weight familiar as coin. He counted them anyway, aloud, because he wanted to hear the figures spoken in that field by somebody, and Fowler waited politely through it and looked at the beck.

"Ten chains," Hale said. "And I took it myself."

"Aye," said Fowler, which committed him to nothing at all.

He wrote the entry there, at the station, standing, with the book open on the wall-top and the ink-horn of iron-gall wedged in the stones: the bearing, the date, the ten chains and the fifty-three links of the short pull beyond, and the description of the mark. Wet ink in a north wind dries slow. He blew on it and turned to the wall.

Two farmers had been leaning on it since the second change, elbows on the coping, watching the chain go out the way men watch a hare. One was grey and one was not. They had been there long enough to have seen every arrow set.

"You'll have seen the line run," Hale said. "It wants two names. You stood here for the taking of it; that's all that's asked."

The grey one looked at the book for a while with real interest, the way a man looks at another man's dog.

"We've no call to be writing in your book," he said.

"It costs you nothing. It says only what you saw."

"Aye," said the other, agreeably, and neither of them moved, and neither of them left, and after a moment the grey one asked after the health of Hale's horse. They were not hostile. That was the thing Hale would set down that evening and then cross out. They stayed at the wall the whole while, and they watched him be refused, and they were sorry about it in a distant way, as one is sorry about weather.

Brock had been there since six. He had come down from Hollins Hall in the dark with a lantern he had not needed by the time he arrived, and he had stood out of the sight-line all morning without once being in the way, and he had a pen.

"You'll want a second hand on that, Mr Hale, and I'm stood here already." He came over the grass, unstoppering his own ink. "I've watched it from the peg. Every arrow of it."

"You have."

"I have." Brock signed, a clear steady agent's hand. "And the lad — you're Ingleford, aren't you? Not dale?"

"Ingleford, sir," said Coulter.

"Then you'll write your name under mine, and mind you do it before Mr Hale steps off this station, or it's worth nothing to anybody."

The boy wrote it, tongue out. Hale had not left the station. He noted that he had not, in the margin, in the same ink.

In the afternoon he walked the line again against the enclosure plan of 1836, unrolled on the wall and held with stones, and here the pleasure of the morning went out of the day. By the plan the distance from the lane corner to the elbow of the beck was rather more than eleven chains. He had it at ten and fifty-three. A surveyor's error, in rough ground, in a bad season, with a stretched chain — he could allow two links, three, five at the outside, and he was generous by nature with other men's arithmetic. He could not allow forty-seven. And where the plan put a field corner, a stone-built corner with an angle of some sixty degrees against the beck, there was no corner, no rubble, no line of different grass, nothing but pasture running unbroken down to the water as though nothing had ever been built there and nothing pulled down.

He stood a long while looking at the place where the corner was not.

At dusk he took the plan to the church, and found Amos Dent in the porch with the door on the latch behind him and the light going off the head of the dale.

"This was drawn in thirty-six," Hale said. "By whom?"

"A gentleman from Kendal way," Dent said. "He was here from the back end of April to about hay time — you'd call it seven weeks. He never walked the bound. It falls at Rogationtide, and he was at his desk that week."

"And after?"

"He went out. He never came back in." Dent looked at the fell and not at Hale. "My father was alive then. Nobody ever told the man why it wasn't confirmed. Nobody thought to."

Hale walked back to the inn with the plan under his arm and sat with his book by the candle, and went through it page by page, counting the names.

There were not many pages yet. Brock's hand was on every one of them but the first.

# Chapter 3 — Identical to the Link

Sunday came up dry, which in that country was an event, and the cloud that had sat on the fell shoulders since Thursday lifted off them like a lid taken from a pot. Hale walked down to Nether Scarrow church with his boots still stiff from the beck and sat at the back, where a surveyor belongs, and where the whole congregation could be counted without turning his head. Forty-one souls. He counted them twice and got forty-one both times, and thought nothing of it at the time except that it was pleasant to be somewhere the numbers behaved.

Amos Dent preached on the Rogation. It was the obvious sermon with the week ahead of them, and he gave it plainly, without oratory, standing square and speaking as though to men he would see later in the day, which he would.

"We go out after the second lesson," he said, "and we are back before the bread has gone cold. There's the length of it. We stop where Josiah Thwaite stopped, and we say the Creed there as he said it, and we go on. Then there's a stretch that takes about as long again, and at the end of that stretch is the place my father put his hand on when I was a lad of nine, and I have put my hand on it every year since, and I shall put my hand on it a week tomorrow. We are asking a blessing on the grass. The grass knows where it is. It's us that has to be reminded."

Hale, who had been trained to hear a description, sat forward.

There was not a direction in it. Not a north, not a south, not a right hand or a left; no up the dale and no down it. There was not a distance in it either — no rood, no chain, no furlong, not so much as a good step. The whole bound of a parish had been laid out from the pulpit in the time it took a clock to move a quarter, and it had been laid out entirely in how long a thing took and who had last done it. Hale caught himself waiting for the number the way one waits for the second boot to drop, and it never dropped, and nobody else in the church appeared to notice its absence. A boy of about eleven in the third pew was nodding along at the right places. He knew where the place my father put his hand on was. Every one of the forty-one knew.

It was, Hale decided, a charming and entirely intelligible country manner, and he was glad of it. A parish that carried its bound in its head like a catechism was a parish that had not let its bound wander. He would put the numbers to it himself and the two accounts would agree, and then they could have the Creed and he could have his plan.

Brock was waiting at the lychgate with two shaved larch poles across his shoulder and a lantern he would not need, having come down at first light on the chance.

"I'd not ask a man to labour on a Sunday," Hale said.

"A pole's not labour, Mr Hale, it's a mark." Brock shifted the larch and smiled. "You'll want a second hand on the entry, and I'm stood here already. The lad's up at the Hall with the flag."

They set the first pole in the peat under the boundary oak at Raven Hause, guyed with three cords and packed with stone, and the second on Sile Head, where the wind had scoured the ground down to grit and the setting took an hour. The air was so clear that Hale could see the whitewash on a byre a full two miles off. He took the instrument to the station he had chosen on the rough ground between, levelled it, and read the angle between the two poles on both verniers, then reversed the telescope and read it again, and the four readings lay within nine seconds of one another, which on that ground with that wind was better than he had any right to. He wrote it in iron-gall ink at the station with the book on his knee. Brock signed under it. Coulter, the Ingleford lad, climbed up from the flag with his cap off and signed under Brock, and Hale blotted the page and only then stood, and only then took the theodolite off its legs and cased it. The poles he left standing. Poles were marks, as Brock said, and marks were meant to stand.

Coming down he was given tea at three farms in turn, at three kitchen tables scrubbed pale, and at the last of them, the high one under the Hause where a widow kept the best grass he had seen in the dale, a scone still too hot to hold. He asked, at each, how far it was to the next house along, out of nothing but the habit of the trade. At the first they told him it was the pipe of a pipe. At the second, that Robert Hird used to do it before his tea went cold and none of them had ever managed it since. At the third the widow considered him for a moment and said her elder boy did it in the time it took her to skim the milk, and would he take another.

He went back to his lodging warm and pleased and did not think about it again.

On the Monday he took the chain out alone. It was slow work single-handed — set the arrow, walk back, sight to the plumb-line, drag the chain forward, and do it again eleven times — and it took him from eight until past two to run the low pasture line he had chained on the Friday with Fowler leading. He knew it was no legal measurement. There were no witnesses at the station, and a figure without two hands to it was a figure for his own satisfaction and nothing else. He wanted his own satisfaction very badly.

Ten chains, fifty-three links.

He stood in the wet grass and looked at the arrows in his fist and felt something come loose in his chest. Then he coiled up and walked it a second time, from the far end back, to take out any bias of his own pacing.

Ten chains, fifty-three links. Identical to the link.

Fowler came down off the intake at five and took the chain from him without being asked and began coiling it in the long practised loops. Hale opened the field book on the wall top and wrote in the margin, in ink, in his own hand:

*Re-measured this day by myself alone, twice, and agreeing exactly. The 1836 plan is 47 links in error over this line. The dale's reputation for crooked measure is slander. Every man who came before me was careless, and I am not.*

He blotted it. Fowler stood with the coiled chain over his forearm and watched him do it, and looked at the page a moment longer than he needed to, and said nothing at all, and went home.

The evening stayed dry. Hale sat up an hour with the book and carried Friday's line and Sunday's angle into the column, and the column summed, and summed again the same when he ran it upward to check. He put out the candle and slept the whole night through without waking once.

# Chapter 4 — The Width of a Field

The mare took the ford at a walk, picking her way over the stones with the water breaking white at her fetlocks, and Hale did not look down at the ford stone as he passed it. He had taken it against the church tower eleven times in five days, one fixed thing sighted to another, and it had closed the same every time. It was the one thing in Scarrowdale he no longer had to think about.

On the far bank he turned in the saddle.

The dale lay behind him in the afternoon light, flat and ordinary. That was the whole of it. From inside, Scarrowdale was a thing of shoulders and hollows, of ground that rose when you expected it to fall, of walls that ran away from a man at angles he had to take twice; from here it was a green wedge between two grey fells with a beck down the middle and a church tower at the foot of it, and it looked no stranger than Wyresdale or Roeburndale or any of the twenty valleys he had chained for the turnpike trust. Cloud sat on the fell shoulders as it always sat. Smoke stood up from Nether Scarrow in three thin columns. He could have covered the whole parish with his thumb.

He thought: it is a small place and I have made too much of it. Then he turned the mare's head for Ingleford and rode on, and did not think of it again until Wednesday.

At Ingleford the standard lay in the market hall, a brass-ended bar bedded in stone that the borough surveyor kept under a hasp, and the borough surveyor was a fat courteous man named Hetherington who had been comparing chains for nineteen years and said so twice. They laid Hale's Gunter's out along the flags. Hetherington went down it link by link with his thumb on the brass, telling the hundred off under his breath, and tried the tally-marks at ten and twenty and fifty, and stretched it, and slackened it, and stretched it again.

"True," he said. "True to the link. You've a good chain, Mr Hale, and it's been kept dry."

"I'd like that written."

"You'd like it written." Hetherington seemed pleased rather than put out, and went to the desk, and wrote it out in a clerk's round hand — *compared this sixteenth day of May 1843 against the borough standard and found true* — and signed it and let the ink dry and did not blot it. Hale folded it once and put it in his breast pocket, against the interim return he had already posted, and felt the small square weight of it there for the rest of the day. A man who can prove his chain is a man who cannot be told his chain is wrong. He slept at the Gate, ate a mutton chop, and thought about the low pasture line with a satisfaction he would have been embarrassed to have named aloud.

He came back over Sile Ford on the Wednesday at three, with the light still high.

Fowler was at the lane corner with Coulter and the arrows, because Fowler was always where he had been told to be. Hale said they would run the low pasture again — the same line, the lane corner to the elbow of the beck — and that he wanted it before the light went. Fowler nodded and took the leading end.

The chain went out. Coulter held; Fowler, leading, set the arrow in the ground at his chain-length and went on, and Coulter drew it as he came up to it; the bracken hissed on the links. Hale walked the line at Coulter's shoulder as he had walked it three times before, and knew the ground now, the tussock at the fourth chain and the soft place where the run-off crossed. At the elbow Fowler stopped and stood, and drew the last arrows out of the ground on his way back, and came and set them in Hale's palm without a word, and Hale counted them in his own hand and read the tally at the chain and took the links himself off the brass.

Eleven chains, seventy-two links.

He stood with the arrows in his hand and the sun on the back of his neck and said, quite evenly, "Again."

They ran it again. Ten chains, ninety-six links.

"Again."

Eleven chains, forty links.

The light was going off Raven Hause when they ran it the fourth time, the shadow coming down the fell face like water finding a level, and Hale made them go fast and did not let Coulter stop to shake the kinks out. Twelve chains, eleven links.

He sat down at the station on the flat stone by the lane corner and opened the field book on his knee.

*TEN CHAINS, FIFTY-THREE LINKS*, in his own iron-gall, Friday's entry, signed at the station by Brock and by Coulter, and under it Monday's two repetitions in his own hand, identical to the link, and the margin.

He did not enter the afternoon's four. He was checking, not recording; he knew the difference, and there was no one at that station to witness a thing taken there but Coulter, and a man does not enter four contradictions into a book he must seal. He set them down on the back of the Ingleford certificate instead, where they had no standing and could do no harm, and added them.

Eleven seventy-two. Ten ninety-six. Eleven forty. Twelve eleven. He added them in the order taken and got forty-six chains, nineteen links, and divided and got a mean of eleven chains, fifty-five links, which was a number belonging to nothing on the ground. He added them backwards to check the carrying and made it forty-six chains, nineteen links again, which proved only that he could add. He grouped them in pairs and the pairs did not agree with each other. He struck out the longest and the shortest and the two that were left were eleven seventy-two and eleven forty and there was no honest way to call those one line. Whatever he did to the column, it would not sum twice alike into anything a man could put on a plan, because four figures that differ are four lines, and he had chained one field.

The chain was true. He had it in writing in his pocket, in a clerk's round hand, from a fat man in Ingleford who had done it for nineteen years.

Fowler coiled the chain. He did it the way he always did it, laying the links over his palm in figures of eight and thumbing them flat, and when it was coiled he set it down by Hale's boot and set the ten arrows beside it in a bundle with the rings together, tidily, within reach of Hale's hand. He had been on the leading end for every run of the afternoon and for the Friday line before it. He looked once at the book open on Hale's knee, and once at Hale, and there was nothing in his face that could be called surprise.

Then he said good evening, sir, and went down the lane to Nether Scarrow, and did not say one word about the figures.

By candlelight in his room at the inn at Nether Scarrow, Hale turned back to Monday's page and read his own margin note through twice. *The dale's reputation for crooked measure is slander, and every man who came before me was careless.* His hand, his ink, at the station, with the light good.

Nothing in his book might be struck through. A correction was a new entry in every respect, and wanted two witnesses who had stood for the taking of the correction itself, and he had no correction to offer them.

He left it standing and went to bed.

# Chapter 5 — First Light on Raven Hause

The parlour fire at Nether Scarrow drew badly in a west wind, and there was a west wind. Brock had the jug and went round with it as though the room were his, which in the way that mattered it was. He filled Coulter's cup, and the carrier's, and Hale's, and came last to Nat Fowler, who had taken the settle end nearest the door and was drying his boots without appearing to.

"Martinmas will be on us before we've done with this," Brock said, pouring. "Your father's ground comes up then, doesn't it, Nat. The yearly." He said it the way a man says the weather is turning. "Hollins Hall likes a useful man. It always has."

Fowler said nothing. Hale, who had eleven pages of the day's work to reduce and a column that had refused him four times, heard the words go past him the way one hears a cart in the lane, and wrote *18 May* at the head of a clean leaf. Tenancies were nothing to him. He had never in his life owned a rood of anything.

He worked until the fire was ash. The sight from Sile Head was unfinished — a ray to the church tower struck and entered, and the second ray, the one that would close the triangle on the oak, still wanting. To break down the instrument now was to lose the whole setting and to begin again tomorrow with a new levelling, a new orientation, a new set of errors to argue with. He had lost three days to arguing with errors, and this unclosed sight would make a fourth.

Nobody in the dale would have left an instrument out. He had been told so, pleasantly, by three separate people who had not quite said why. It was custom, and custom was not law, and law was what he was paid for. He climbed back up in the last of it with a blanket rolled under his arm, checked the plumb and the levels, laid a stone at each foot of the tripod, and sat down beside it in his coat.

The cloud came onto the fell about eleven. He did not sleep so much as hold still while the hours went over him. His boots filled. There was a moment somewhere in the small hours when the wet had gone through to his shirt and he thought quite clearly: *this is what the note at Midsummer costs, and it is not too much.* Then a long grey while of nothing, and then the shape of the theodolite standing above him against a sky that had begun to be a sky.

A light came up the fell, swinging, and went out.

"You'll have had a poor night of it," said Brock, out of the dark, from perhaps twenty yards. He had the lantern in his left hand with the flame just killed and Hale's field book under his right arm, flat against his coat to keep the wet off it. "I thought you'd want this. A man wakes up on a hill without his book and he's lost half of what he saw."

Hale got up. His knees were not his own. "You're early."

"I'm always early. It's the only economy I have." Brock was already looking east, to the hause, where the fell shoulder had begun to separate itself from the cloud. "It'll be on Raven Hause in a quarter of an hour. There's no sense standing in the dark when it's coming."

They walked across. Hale remembered that walk afterwards in every particular: the bracken soaking him to the thigh, the peat sucking at his heel on the second crossing of the runnel, the cold gone so far into his hands that he had to work them under his arms as he went, and Brock talking the whole way in that even, warm, procedural voice — the state of the Ingleford road, a dispute over a hog, what the Commission would want and in what order it would want it. He remembered coming up to the station under the boundary oak with the light standing on the fell, actually on it, the grass going from grey to a wet yellow-green around their boots and the oak putting a shadow west of itself for the first time that day. He remembered Fowler there with the flag already planted, and the Reverend Amos Dent a little apart with his hat in his hand and his coat buttoned to the chin, and thinking, with a distant professional satisfaction, that Brock had contrived to have two signing hands on a fellside at four in the morning, and that this was what the man was for.

He remembered the oak, and the tower away down the dale catching it, and the angle between them, which was an angle he could have taken half-asleep, and which was true; those two had closed on one another in every survey ever made.

He remembered the cold.

He did not remember the pen. But there was no moment at which he looked for it, so there was nothing, then, to miss.

By the middle of the morning he was back on Sile Head with the cloud lifting off it, and the theodolite stood where he had left it, every foot on its stone, the plumb bob hanging quiet. It was pointing at the church tower.

He stopped six feet short of it and did what he would have done anywhere on earth: he walked a circle round the tripod at two paces, and then at one, reading the ground. Cropped grass, wet, laid over from the night's weather, and laid all one way — the way the wind had gone. No heel. No toe. No print of a hand or a knee. Nothing dragged and nothing pressed. He knelt and put his face close to the near foot and the stone under it had not shifted in its bed; the moss round the stone was unbroken.

He looked along the telescope. The cross hairs sat on the tower, near enough, off perhaps by a hair to the north.

He wrote, standing, *Instrument found undisturbed in position, telescope bearing on Nether Scarrow tower. No marks.* Then he broke it down and carried it off the hill, and did not think about it, because there was nothing in his training that told him what to think.

It was evening, at the parlour table, going back through the book to reduce the week, that he came to a Day 9 entry he did not know he had.

It was in his own hand. Not an imitation of his hand — his hand, tired, the *R* of Raven with the long tail it got when he was cold, the figures cramped the way they always went when he wrote standing. An angle taken at the Raven Hause station, oak to tower, closed and entered. Below it, in the plain words he used for such things, the head of the parish carried to Raven Hause.

Beneath that, Nat Fowler's mark, witnessed and named. Beneath that, in a small upright clerical hand, *Amos Dent, Incumbent.*

Nowhere on the leaf was Silas Brock's name. Hale looked for it twice. Its absence troubled him and he could not have said, if asked, on what grounds.

He took up the pen to strike the entry through, and stopped with the nib an inch off the page, because a line drawn through a signed entry was a correction, and a correction was a new entry in every respect, and a new entry required two witnesses who had stood at that station for the taking of the correction itself, and the men who had signed the original counted for nothing toward it even if they were the same two men.

He put the pen down. Then he drew a loose sheet towards him and wrote the rule out in full, clause by clause, to see whether it would look different in his own writing.

It did not. It meant that he could not lawfully touch his own book until two people willing to sign stood with him under the oak.

# Chapter 6 — What Is Written Can Be Taken

She saw him from the barn door when he was still only a dark stroke on the track, and she knew him by the way he carried the book: under the arm, level, the way a man carries something he will not let get wet.

Hannah Rigg went in and set the kettle on the crane and swung it over. The fire had been banked since morning and wanted rousing, so she roused it. Her younger boy was at the trough and she told him to stop where he was and not to come in, and he did not ask why, because he had learned that much.

By the time the surveyor's boots came into the yard the water was singing. That was the whole of the courtesy, and it cost nothing, and she had been doing it to men like him since she was nineteen.

"Mrs Rigg."

"Mr Hale. Get that coat off before it gets into you."

He got it off. He was wet to the shoulders and had the look men got up here in their second week, when the cloud stopped being weather and started being a room they lived in. He sat where she pointed him, which was the settle by the fire and not the chair at the table, and he put the field book on his knee and not on her cloth.

She poured. He watched her pour, and she let him.

"I'm obliged to you," he said. "I'll not keep you above a quarter of an hour. I want the extent of your ground."

"There's a scone there, and butter."

"Thank you." He took one. He was hungry and trying not to be seen to be. "The extent of your ground, Mrs Rigg."

"My lads mow it in three days," she said, "if the weather holds and if the little one doesn't take a scythe to his own leg again."

He set the scone down. "That is a rate of work. It is not an extent."

"It's what I've got."

"Then put it another way for me. A man walking the top wall of it — how long is he at it?"

"He's at it from the milking to the milking, if he stops to look, and they always stop to look." She sat down across from him with her own cup and did not drink from it. "My husband used to do it before his breakfast. He was a quick walker and a poor eater."

Hale wrote nothing. He had a way of not writing that was as deliberate as writing. "I cannot enter three days' mowing in a field book."

"No," she agreed. "I don't suppose you can."

In her head it was seven acres and a rood in the Hollins intake, and eleven and a half in the Lang Riggs, and the little one under the scar was four and some perches she had never bothered to settle because her father had never bothered. She knew it the way she knew the stairs in the dark. It sat in her like a stone in a shoe and it did not come up her throat, and it never had, and she had long ago stopped noticing that it never had.

"There's a thing I'd tell you," she said instead, "while you've the tea in your hands."

"Say it."

"My eldest was up Thursday night into Friday with a ewe that was going to die and didn't. He was in and out of the low fold till the light came." She turned her cup a quarter round on the table. "He saw Mr Brock pass. Then he saw him pass again. Before the light, both times, and going by he had a lantern lit, which was fair enough, for it was black as a shut byre. Coming back it had greyed off enough that a body could see his own feet, and the lantern was still burning. That's what stuck in the lad. A careful man like that, burning oil he'd no use for."

Hale had gone very still, in the way of a man who has found something and does not yet know which pocket to put it in. "Before first light."

"Before it."

"Your son is certain of that."

"He's certain the ewe didn't die. The rest he's certain of the same road."

"Did he speak to him?"

"He did not. You don't, at that hour." She got up and lifted the kettle off. "I'm not telling you what it means, Mr Hale. I don't know what it means. I'm telling you the lad saw it and it's stuck in him, and I'd not have it stick in him for nothing."

He looked at the fire for a while. He did not write that down either, and she thought better of him for it. Then he said, "Thank you," and nothing more, and she was glad, because she had no more of it to give and did not want to be asked for what she hadn't.

"Come out," she said. "The rain's given over."

They went out through the top gate and along the wall with the beck talking away under them, and the cloud lifting off the shoulders the way it does at the end of a wet day, grudging, showing the ground in pieces. She took him to the first gate and stopped.

"That one's the Hollins intake. My grandfather's father took it in. That one beyond, with the lambing wall, is the Lang Riggs. And yon under the scar is the Little Waste, which is a joke, and the joke's on me now."

"They are good grass," Hale said.

"They're the only good grass I've got. Everything else is ground that grows stone."

"They're on no plan I have," he said. "Estate, enclosure, turnpike, county. Not one of the four."

"No," said Hannah Rigg. "They wouldn't be."

She put her hand on the gate and looked at the Lang Riggs, where the wall ran up and the light came along it, and she wanted to say to him: *stand there and I'll tell you it to the yard.* The wanting arrived whole and clear and went nowhere, the way water goes nowhere in a stopped spout. She went round it.

"Now hear what I'm asking you to hear," she said. "If the head of the parish is put at the oak, and the tops are entered waste of the manor — that's the words, waste of the manor, they'll be Mr Brock's words — then these three are not in the parish's fields at all. They're rough grazing, and the rough grazing is Hollins Hall's. My hay. My lads' three days. At Lady Day I'm a trespasser on it and they can have me off, and they'll do it kindly, with a letter, and they'll be sorry."

Hale said nothing for a moment. Then: "Then they must be numbered."

"Numbered."

"There is no other remedy. The Commission confirms nothing that lies outside the bound as walked at Rogationtide and signed by the incumbent. A field outside that walk cannot be numbered at all — not by me, not by anyone after me. Inside it, I can number them. But understand what that is, Mrs Rigg." He turned to face her. "Numbered is tithed. It is a figure in a book at Somerset House, and a figure on a plan with a seal on it, and it is there after you and after your sons and after their sons. It does not come off again. Your people have kept this dale out of that for a hundred years, and I am telling you plainly that I would be the man who puts you in it."

She thought of Amos Dent then, and the chest, and the book in it, and how easily a woman might ask. And she thought what asking costs, and who ends up holding the other end of it, and she set the thought down where she had set it down before.

"Number them," she said.

He looked at her. "You are sure."

"I'm forty-six and I've buried a husband and I can count," said Hannah Rigg. "Number them."

She left him at the gate and went back down for the kettle, because it would want filling again before the lads came in. At the door she turned. The three of them lay above the beck in the last of the light, green as anything in England, and there was nothing written on them anywhere in England at all.

# Chapter 7 — Durations and Dead Men

The perambulation book had lain at the bottom of his own box for eleven days, under the spare arrows and a coil of whipcord, and on Sunday morning Hale took it out and set it on the parlour table at the inn and opened it because there was nothing else left to open.

It was not a survey. He had half expected the vicar's neat Durham hand to have smuggled some figures in, a chain here, a furlong there, and there were none. There were no figures at all. The bound of the parish of Nether Scarrow was recorded in how long it took to walk and in the names of men who had died.

*From the ford stone, the time of a short psalm to the thorn where Jonas Hird stood.* *From Hird's thorn, by the gate, the time of the Creed said through, to the sheepfold that was Wilfrid Tatham's.* *Above Tatham's fold, going wide of the three intakes, the time it takes to say the Lord's Prayer twice, to the great oak.*

Going wide of the three intakes. He turned back. 1789, another hand, browner ink: *out beyond the three intakes above the beck, as always*. 1751: *without the intakes*. 1703, the earliest, the letters cramped and the spelling loose, and there it was again — the walk went out round the ground above the beck and came back to the oak, and had done so in every hand for a hundred and forty years, and not one of those hands had written a single number to say how far out.

Hale sat with his thumb on the page for a long while. The Commission would not have called it evidence. The Commission would have called it folklore, and apportioned by estimate, and been wrong by three intakes. But it was signed, every walk of it, by the incumbent of the day, and the rule stood plain in the printed instructions in his own bag: no field outside the walked bound could be numbered, and the walked bound was what the incumbent signed.

The dale had kept the only record that could not be argued with, and had kept it in a form no surveyor would stoop to read.

He closed the book and went to find Fowler.

They went up together after the morning service, not speaking, the bracken wet through to his knees inside a hundred yards. The boundary oak at Raven Hause stood where it had always stood, and looked, as it always did, like a thing that had been put there rather than grown.

"Friday," Hale said. "First light. Tell me what you saw."

"Mr Brock came up," Fowler said. He was looking at the oak.

"Before Mr Brock came up. Was I awake?"

"You were on your feet, sir."

"That is not what I asked." Hale set the theodolite case down in the heather. "Did I speak to you? Did I give you an instruction — any instruction — before that entry was made?"

Fowler considered the oak. "You had your book," he said.

"I had my book." Hale heard his own voice go flat and did not trouble to mend it. "Nat. I am not asking you for a distance and I am not asking you to name a direction. I am asking you what you put your mark to and why you put it there."

The wind came over the hause and turned the bracken silver and turned it back.

"I put my mark to what was set in front of me," Fowler said. "The angle on the oak was true." He did not shift his eyes. "And Mr Brock had spoken of Martinmas the night before."

Hale waited for more, and there was no more, because there was no more. Fowler did not add that he was sorry. He did not say that his father was sixty-one and held his ground by the year and would not get another year anywhere in the hundred. He did not ask to be understood. He had given three facts, in order, and every one of them was true, and together they were worse than a confession would have been, because a confession could have been disputed.

"Thank you," Hale said.

"That's what's in your hand, sir," Fowler said. "I'll not say it for you."

Hale set up over the oak because there was nothing else to try and because he had woken with the thought and been unable to put it down. He levelled the plates, and swung, and brought the cross onto the church tower at Nether Scarrow, four miles down the dale and grey in the morning, and read, and wrote. He swung to the ford stone at the mouth of the Sile and read, and wrote. He closed the round back onto the tower.

The three angles closed on themselves to the second.

He read them again. They closed. He struck the instrument, reset it, and did the whole round a third time, and it closed, and he stood in the wet with his hand on the limb and something in his chest going over like a cart on a bank.

Eleven days. Eleven days of columns that would not sum twice alike, of the same wall measuring four different lengths between breakfast and dinner, of his certified chain telling him lies in good faith. And here were three things — a tower, a stone in a ford, an oak — that agreed with themselves and with each other and, he understood with absolute clarity, would agree for any man who ever came here with a glass, and had agreed for the four honest fools whose four honest plans disagreed about everything else. They had each measured a different dale. Their dales had answered them, and gone quiet, and told the next man something else. His own lines had stopped repeating the hour he rode out over Sile Ford and came back a stranger to his own arithmetic. That was all it was. He said it to himself once, flatly, and let it go.

And the instrument on Sile Head, turned in the dark to face the tower with no mark in the grass at its feet — he had taken that for a warning, and lain awake calling it one. It was not a warning. He had left it with a sight unfinished and it had settled, the way water settles into the beck, onto the one direction that was not in dispute. He understood it now as an instruction: look there. It was easier to think the thing had been telling him where to look all week than to think there was no reason in it at all, and he took the easier thought, knowing what he was doing, and stood there holding it while the wind came over.

Relief went through him, and directly behind the relief, cold as the ground, came the other thing: the dale had been answering him helpfully the whole time.

"I thought I should find you up," Brock said.

He came the last of the slope with his coat over his arm and his colour high, entirely pleasant, and out of his satchel he drew a roll of parchment and opened it on the flat stone by the oak with two pebbles to hold the corners. A fair copy. Engrossed — properly engrossed, an office hand, the columns ruled, the upper pastures set down as waste of the manor in a clerk's beautiful letters.

"It wants nothing but your seal," Brock said. "It would save you the Rogation walk, which is four hours of wet, and it would save you the delay, which I think you can afford less than I can. Your note falls at Midsummer, Hale. I do not say that to press you. I say it because it is true and we are both men of business."

Hale looked at the parchment for a while.

"No," he said.

Brock waited, warm, patient, a half-step ahead as always, for the reason.

Hale gave him none. He knelt and began to pack the theodolite into its case, and after a moment Brock rolled the copy up, carefully, so as not to crack the ink, and said something civil about the weather turning, and went down.

The light was going off Raven Hause when he reached the church, which meant it was going off everywhere at once, and Dent was in the porch with the key in his hand.

"Tomorrow," Hale said, "I will take a new entry at the station at the oak. Not a correction endorsed on the old one — a fresh taking, at the station, and two witnesses who have stood there for the taking of it, signing before I leave the ground. The men who signed on Friday count for nothing toward it. I want that understood by whoever comes."

Dent turned the key over in his fingers.

"I'll sign a bound I have walked," he said. "And I'll sign it once."

"Once is all I want."

The vicar locked the door and tried it, as he did every night, and looked up past the tower to where the fell had gone the colour of ash.

"We start," he said, "when the light is on the fell. Not before."

# Chapter 8 — The Walked Bound

They came out of the church porch at eight with the cloud sitting low on the fell shoulders, and Amos Dent went first with the perambulation book open across his forearms like a man carrying water.

He read as he walked. Hale had expected mumbling and got none: Dent's voice went out over the wet bracken clear enough to reach the back of the line, where the Ingleford lad Coulter carried the arrows in a bundle because nobody would let him count them aloud. *From the ford stone, the time it takes to say the Creed twice, to the thorn that Simeon Rigg's father grubbed out and his son set again. From the thorn, the time it takes a woman to fill a kist with peat, to the intake wall that Joseph Dent kept.* Names of dead men, and how long the walking took, and not once in two hours a distance.

Hale walked at Dent's shoulder with his field book buttoned under his coat and understood at last, with a kind of vertigo, that there was nothing in the book for Dent to break himself on. A hundred and forty years of hands had kept it so. They had written the bound in durations and in the dead precisely so that it could be said out loud by people who could not say a distance, and Dent reading it to the whole parish was not an exception to the dale's silence. It was the silence working, in public, on its one appointed morning.

Nat Fowler walked in the body of the line with his hat off. Nobody spoke to him and nobody kept away from him. His father's tenancy came up at Martinmas whatever happened on this hill.

At the top of the dale, where the track bent in under the scree towards Raven Hause, Hannah Rigg went straight on.

She did not announce it. She simply held her line where the path turned, out along the lip above the beck, round the Hollins intake and the Lang Riggs and the Little Waste, three green shelves of hay in a country of rush and stone. Dent read on without a check. Behind him the line bent, sixty souls of Scarrowdale turning out wide after her through wet grass to the knee, and not one voice said that this was not the way. Brock walked it with them, at the back, hands behind him, watching the ground.

It took forty minutes longer than the old way. Hale counted nothing and said nothing, and let them walk.

At the boundary oak they stopped. It stood as it had always stood, and it had measured the same for every surveyor who had ever put a glass on it, and it would measure the same for the next.

Rigg came up to the trunk and laid her right hand flat against the bark, fingers spread, and held it there.

She did not look at him. She did not say a word. Hale understood what he was being given and went back twenty yards to the instrument without thanking her for it, because thanking her would have made it a favour, and set the theodolite, and took the angle off the back of her hand where it lay on the oak. Her arm did not tremble. It was raining lightly. He read the vernier, and read it again, and wrote the figure standing there, and she took her hand down and shook the wet off it and went to stand with her sons.

Then the station at Raven Hause, with the light still on the fell.

He was careful out loud, for the benefit of anybody who might one day read the sheet. This was a fresh taking, here, now: he said so. He shot the round again from this station — tower, ford stone, oak — with Rigg standing at his left elbow and Dent at his right, and both of them stayed through the whole of it, the setting, the sighting, the booking. The Friday entry was lawful and would not be scratched out. He wrote a new one under it in iron-gall, that the head of the parish stood at the boundary oak by the bound as walked at Rogationtide this day, and that the three intakes above the beck lay within it, and he did not lift his hand until it was finished.

Rigg signed. Dent signed. They signed as witnesses who had stood at that station for the taking of this entry and nothing else; Dent's Friday signature counted for nothing toward it and Fowler's mark counted for nothing toward it, and Hale did not ask Fowler to come near the book. He watched them both put pen down before he touched the tripod. The light was still up on the fell above them, greying, but up.

He carried the instrument off Raven Hause in the dusk with his hands shaking, and the shaking was not fear.

Tuesday he began again from nothing. Church tower, ford stone, boundary oak: the three that hold, angles taken directly among them and no other line trusted to carry weight. Everything else in Scarrowdale he hung off that triangle like washing off a rope. He worked from six until four in the vestry with the plan weighted down by candlesticks, numbering every field that lay inside the bound as the parish had walked it — and the Hollins intake, the Lang Riggs and the Little Waste were inside it, and so they could be numbered, and being numbered they would be tithed, and being tithed they were Hannah Rigg's beyond any agent's argument forever.

He added the columns at half past four. He added them again at five. The two totals were the same.

He sat with that a while. It was the first honest sum he had made since he rode out over Sile Ford, and what it bought was the dale on paper at last, every green shelf of it, numbered in a book at Somerset House that would outlive her and outlive her sons.

Dent signed the bound he had walked. Once.

Brock was the first man to his hand. He came across the churchyard with his hat already off, said it was a good plan and honestly got, shook once, and settled the survey's bills at the inn to the penny before Hale's horse was brought round — chainmen, candles, the lad's boots, everything. He did not complain. He did not look up the dale.

Hale rode out at seven with the fee assured and the note answerable at Midsummer.

At Sile Ford he stopped and did the only thing left to him that meant anything, and measured the stone. Four feet two inches and a half above the water: as near as his first guess had put it on the day he rode in, and exactly what it would give anybody who ever asked it. The three constants did not care who held the chain.

Everything else he had drawn was true, and sealed, and would stand — and would never measure so again for him, because he had gone out once already and come back, and the dale did not offer that twice. If he ever rode in over this ford, not one line of it would repeat.

He turned the horse up the Ingleford road and did not look back.
